To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Ca2+ is required for the activation of CRAC channels, and that this activation is voltage dependent.
Ca2+ is a cofactor that is required for the activation of CRAC channels in T lymphocyte plasma membranes.
Ca(2+), acting at an extracellular site, can potentiate store-operated Ca(2+) channels in T lymphocyte membranes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms underlying the activation and regulation of Ca(2+)(i)-dependent Ca(2+)-(in) channels in T-lymphocytes.
the mechanisms that regulate the influx of extracellular Ca(2+) through store-operated channels.
understanding the molecular mechanisms that underlie Ca(2+)(i) homeostasis and Ca(2+)-(dependent) gene expression in T cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ca(2+) is an obligatory coactivator of CRAC channel activation.
CDP is a Ca2+-dependent process, which occurs in the plasma membrane, is independent of intracellular Ca buffering, and is voltage dependent.
the store-depleting signal by itself triggers the opening of only a small fraction (approximately 50%) of the capacitative Ca2+-entry channels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the depletion of Ca2+ from internal stores triggers the opening, in part, of Ca2+ channels in the plasma membranes.
the depletion of intracellular calcium stores triggers the opening and subsequent potentiation of store operated calcium channels.

Ca2+ entry into T lymphocytes is regulated by two distinct mechanisms, a store-depletion signal that activates the Ca2+ release activated Ca2+ (or CRAC) channels and a Ca2+ influx signal that potentiates the activity of the CRAC channels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca2+ is a key cofactor for the activation of store-operated Ca2+ entry.
Ca(2+)(o) potentiates CRAC channels in Jurkat T lymphocytes, and this potentiation is not mediated by an intracellular Ca(2+), but rather by Ca(2+) binding to an extracellular site.
CRAC channel activation requires two signals.
